name: Vitamin K cream

lead: Vitamin K creams contain vitamin K, usually K1 (phylloquinone), and are marketed to reduce the bluish or purplish look of under-eye circles and bruising. People try them for a lighter, clearer under-eye.

The theory is that dark circles from visible blood vessels or small leaks of blood pigment can fade if vitamin K supports clotting locally. Vitamin K's recognized medical uses are systemic, such as preventing bleeding in newborns and reversing excess warfarin effect; the sources reviewed did not describe topical use for dark circles as established.

paras: People use it as an eye cream or serum, applied under the eyes daily, often within a broader eye-care routine. Any change is usually judged over weeks, and many combine it with sunscreen and concealer.

Cosmetic creams can cause skin irritation in sensitive people. Orally, no toxicity has been documented for K1 or K2; intravenous K1 has caused rare severe allergic-type reactions. People on blood thinners such as warfarin are typically told to discuss vitamin K with their clinician.

angle.text: It is marketed in eye creams for dark circles with a vascular component and for bruising, and users apply it under the eyes aiming for a lighter look. The idea is that topical K fades vascular discoloration. Its established medical roles are systemic.

lead: Vitamin K cream is a cosmetic or topical product containing vitamin K, usually phylloquinone (K1), used on the skin to improve the look of bruises and of under-eye circles that have a vascular (bluish or purplish) component. People apply it to the thin skin beneath the eyes, to post-procedure bruising and to spider veins, aiming for a clearer, less discoloured complexion.

Vitamin K is a family of fat-soluble vitamins whose recognised medical roles are systemic: it is a cofactor that makes clotting proteins functional, and it is given to prevent bleeding in newborns and to reverse excess warfarin effect.[1] The reasoning behind topical use is that a clotting-supportive vitamin could limit blood pooling or leakage that shows through thin skin.

Human trials of topical vitamin K have mostly looked at bruising after laser or oculofacial procedures. An American Academy of Ophthalmology review of 11 studies of homeopathic agents and vitamins for post-surgical bruising found that in two studies vitamin K cream performed equivalently to placebo; a small split-face laser trial found no significant difference when the cream was used before treatment, and a randomised trial of wound healing after electrocautery found faster healing with 1 percent vitamin K cream than with a moisturiser.[2][3][4]

paras: Henrik Dam found in 1929 that chicks fed a fat-depleted diet bled, and proposed a missing coagulation factor; the letter K derives from the German word for coagulation. Dam and Edward Doisy shared the 1943 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work.[1]
The vitamin is a cofactor in making clotting proteins such as prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X functional.[1]

Eye products containing vitamin K are marketed for under-eye discolouration. Wikipedia's dark-circle article lists several causes, including thin skin that shows vessels, pigmentation, allergy, iron deficiency and sleep loss, and names caffeine and vitamin C among cosmetic remedies; vitamin K is not mentioned there.[5]

Bruising after laser treatment of facial telangiectases and after eyelid surgery is the setting where topical vitamin K has been tested most, because bruises are visible and fade over about two weeks.

High oral intakes of K1 and K2 have no known toxicity and regulators in the US, Japan and the EU have not set upper limits. Intravenous K1 can cause serious anaphylactoid reactions in about 3 per 10,000 treatments, mostly linked to a castor-oil solubilizer. Synthetic menadione (K3) was banned as a supplement in the US because of allergic reactions and hemolytic anemia.[1] These figures concern systemic use, not cosmetic creams.
A 2015 study of vitamin K cream used to reduce injection-site reactions in people with multiple sclerosis who inject interferon beta describes topical use on the skin in a clinical setting.[6]

A 2002 double-blind trial in 22 patients applied vitamin K cream to one half of the face and vehicle to the other before or after pulsed dye laser treatment for facial telangiectases; pre-treatment use showed no significant difference in bruising compared with placebo.[2] A 2010 randomised, rater-blinded trial created laser bruises on volunteers' arms and compared 5 percent vitamin K, a vitamin K and retinol preparation, 20 percent arnica and white petrolatum, finding a significant overall difference between treatments, with arnica improving bruising more than petrolatum.[4]

The 2022 American Academy of Ophthalmology review found that in two controlled studies topical vitamin K was equivalent to placebo for bruising after oculofacial or laser surgery, while perioperative arnica provided negligible benefit over placebo in seven controlled studies.[3] A 2019 randomised trial in 63 patients found that 1 percent vitamin K cream produced significantly better wound contraction and time to recovery than a Eucerin control after electrocautery, with healing time not differing from a phenytoin cream.[7] Studies in rats reported faster wound repair with topical vitamin K.[8] No trial has tested vitamin K cream specifically for under-eye dark circles.

timeline.event: Henrik Dam reports a dietary factor needed for blood coagulation, later named vitamin K.[1]
Dam and Edward Doisy share the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on vitamin K.[1]
Randomised split-face trial of topical vitamin K for laser-induced bruising is published.[2]
Randomised trial reports faster wound healing with 1 percent vitamin K cream after electrocautery.[7]
American Academy of Ophthalmology reviews homeopathic agents and vitamins for bruising after oculofacial surgery.[3]
